article_title: Implementing Positive Behavior Interventions and Supports during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Three Tiers of Prevention and Intervention as Protective Factors
citation: Gage, N. A., Grasley-Boy, N. M., MacSuga-Gage, A. S., & Ulrich, T. G. (2025). Implementing Positive Behavior Interventions and Supports During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Three Tiers of Prevention and Intervention as Protective Factors. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: PBIS three-tiered prevention and intervention framework
description: PBIS is described as "a three-tiered, comprehensive, evidence-based framework aimed at improving and integrating all the data, systems, and practices that shape student outcomes." It organizes supports into universal Tier 1 schoolwide expectations taught and positively reinforced for all students, targeted Tier 2 small-group social skills supports such as Check In–Check Out for roughly 5–15 percent of students, and intensive individualized Tier 3 supports based on functional behavior assessment for 3–5 percent of students. It is a framework supporting ongoing professional development and capacity building, not a curriculum or scripted program.
requirements: Schools identify a leadership team, secure staff buy-in, evaluate data systems, identify training and coaching resources, develop an action plan, and monitor and adjust implementation, including completing the Tiered Fidelity Inventory
constraints: The article states universal Tier 1 PBIS is designed to prevent challenging behavior but not designed to address needs that are more intensive
target_learners: All students in a school, with Tier 2 supports for the approximately 5–15 percent nonresponsive to Tier 1 and Tier 3 supports for the 3–5 percent needing individualized intervention
target_learning_goals: Improving social, emotional, behavioral, and academic outcomes for all students and reducing disciplinary exclusions
examples: A midwestern state has trained over 800 schools in more than 280 districts since 2005 using a 2-year cohort model, representing 44 percent of all schools statewide
key_sources: Gage, N. A., Grasley-Boy, N. M., MacSuga-Gage, A. S., & Ulrich, T. G. (2025). Implementing Positive Behavior Interventions and Supports During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Three Tiers of Prevention and Intervention as Protective Factors. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673553

article_title: 'Advancing Problem-Based Learning in Biomedical Engineering in the Era of Generative AI'
citation: Micky C. Nnamdi, J. Ben Tamo, Benoit Marteau, Wenqi Shi, May D. Wang. (2026). Advancing Problem-Based Learning in Biomedical Engineering in the Era of Generative AI. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16558
title: AI guardrails policy set for PBL courses
description: A five-part guardrail package governing student GenAI use in PBL courses: tool restrictions, data protection, disclosure and validation, code provenance, and equity of access. The article states that "Teams documented when and how they used AI tools, validated AI outputs for accuracy and bias, and anchored all literature claims in primary sources rather than AI-generated text." Approved tools (e.g., Copilot, Zoom AI Companion, Teams Premium) were provided to ensure equitable access, AI-assisted code segments were marked with comments, and no PII or protected health information could be submitted to any AI tool.
requirements: Institutional AI-use guidance permitting GenAI under privacy and security review
Disclosure logs documenting when and how AI tools were used
constraints: Banned software or tools such as DeepSeek were prohibited; only institutionally approved tools were allowed
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in biomedical AI courses
examples: Teams marked AI-assisted code with provenance comments and anchored literature claims in primary sources during the 2021–2023 offerings

article_title: 'Problem-Based Learning and the Structural Conditions for Productive AI Integration'
citation: Michael Rowe. (2026). Problem-based learning and the structural conditions for productive AI integration. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/haet3_v1
title: Structural alignment of PBL's core features with the conditions for productive AI integration
description: The essay's central framework: problem-based learning's four defining structural features — problem-driven inquiry, collaborative knowledge construction, facilitation over instruction, and metacognitive reflection — are the same conditions under which AI integration becomes educationally productive rather than substitutive. The alignment is claimed to be structural, not retrospective, since PBL was designed around these conditions before AI existed. The essay states: "PBL's structural features are the conditions for productive AI integration." The argument extends beyond PBL to any pedagogy sharing these features.
requirements: A pedagogy must share the structural features: problem-driven inquiry, collaborative knowledge construction, facilitation over instruction, and metacognitive reflection
constraints: The argument concerns what PBL was designed to create, not what every programme empirically delivers; it produces theoretical warrant, not empirical proof; the author declares a prior commitment to PBL-compatible pedagogy
target_learners: health professions students in higher education
examples: The essay traces the alignment to PBL's origins at McMaster University as a response to transmission-based curricula, citing Barrows (1986) and Norman & Schmidt (1992)
key_sources: Michael Rowe. (2026). Problem-based learning and the structural conditions for productive AI integration. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/haet3_v1

citation: Bradshaw, C. P., Koth, C. W., Thornton, L. A., & Leaf, P. J. (2009). Altering School Climate through School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports: Findings from a Group-Randomized Effectiveness Trial. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-008-0114-9
title: School-wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS)
description: PBIS is a universal, school-wide prevention strategy aimed at reducing disruptive behavior problems, described in the article as "a universal, school-wide prevention strategy that is currently implemented in over 7,500 schools". It operates as a whole-school prevention model whose implementation was tested in a group-randomized effectiveness trial in 37 elementary schools, where trained schools varied in how quickly they adopted the model. The article treats PBIS as an organizational as well as behavioral intervention, linking it to staff-reported school climate.
requirements: School-wide adoption across the whole school rather than a classroom-level program
Implementation fidelity monitoring, which the article found necessary to detect effects on some organizational dimensions
constraints: Effects on collegial leadership and institutional integrity were significant only when implementation fidelity was included in the model
target_learning_goals: improve school organizational health and climate
examples: A group-randomized controlled effectiveness trial assigned 37 elementary schools to trained versus comparison conditions over 5 years

article_title: Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?
citation: Hmelo-Silver, C.E. (2004). Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?. Educational Psychology Review, 16, 235–266. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:EDPR.0000034022.16470.f3
title: Problem-based learning as an instructional method of learning through facilitated problem solving
description: The article defines problem-based learning (PBL) as an instructional method in which "students learn through facilitated problem solving." Learning centers on "a complex problem that does not have a single correct answer." Students work in collaborative groups to identify what they need to learn, engage in self-directed learning, apply new knowledge to the problem, and reflect on what they learned and on the effectiveness of the strategies employed. The teacher acts to facilitate the learning process rather than to provide knowledge. The article presents this as a constructivist, experience-based approach with a long history in problem-based approaches to learning.
requirements: A complex problem without a single correct answer around which student learning is organized
A teacher who facilitates the learning process rather than providing knowledge directly
examples: The article describes the PBL cycle: students identify learning needs in collaborative groups, engage in self-directed learning, apply new knowledge to the problem, and reflect on learning and strategy effectiveness.
key_sources: Hmelo-Silver, C.E. (2004). Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?. Educational Psychology Review, 16, 235–266. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:EDPR.0000034022.16470.f3

article_title: Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?
citation: Hmelo-Silver, C.E. (2004). Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?. Educational Psychology Review, 16, 235–266. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:EDPR.0000034022.16470.f3
title: Five goals of problem-based learning
description: The article enumerates five goals of PBL: "1) flexible knowledge, 2) effective problem-solving skills, 3) SDL skills, 4) effective collaboration skills, and 5) intrinsic motivation." This goal framework organizes the article's examination of the nature of learning in PBL and its review of empirical evidence. The framework distinguishes content knowledge goals (flexible knowledge) from strategy goals (problem solving, self-directed learning), social goals (collaboration), and affective goals (intrinsic motivation).
requirements: Instruction organized around complex problems that engage students in collaborative, self-directed work
constraints: The article notes considerable research exists on the first three goals but little on the last two
examples: The article structures its review of empirical evidence around these five goals, noting the evidence base differs across them.

title: In PBL the teacher facilitates learning rather than providing knowledge
description: The article states that in PBL "the teacher acts to facilitate the learning process rather than to provide knowledge." This facilitation role supports students as they work through complex problems in collaborative groups, identify their learning needs, engage in self-directed learning, and reflect on their learning and strategies. The principle positions the instructor as a guide to the problem-solving and self-directed learning process rather than as a primary source of content transmission.
requirements: Instructors skilled in facilitation of collaborative problem solving and self-directed learning
examples: The article describes the teacher's facilitation role as integral to the PBL cycle of problem solving, self-directed learning, application, and reflection.

title: PBL learning cycle: problem solving, self-directed learning, application, and reflection
description: The article describes a recurring instructional sequence in PBL: "Students work in collaborative groups to identify what they need to learn in order to solve a problem. They engage in self-directed learning (SDL) and then apply their new knowledge to the problem and reflect on what they learned and the effectiveness of the strategies employed." This cycle organizes learning around a complex problem, alternates collaborative identification of learning needs with individual self-directed study, and closes with reflection on both content and strategy effectiveness.

Collaborative groups
Opportunities for self-directed learning between group sessions

article_title: Supporting Student Self-Regulated Learning in Problem- and Project-Based Learning
citation: Mary C. English, Anastasia Kitsantas. (2013). Supporting Self-Regulated Learning in Problem- and Project-Based Learning. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-based Learning. https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1339
title: A theoretical model of the relationship between PBL and self-regulated learning
description: The article presents a theoretical model linking problem- and project-based learning environments to students' self-regulated learning. The model organizes how PBL contexts and teaching practices relate to the SRL processes students must deploy — "setting goals, monitoring, reflecting, and sustaining their motivation" — across the phases of a PBL project. It serves as the framework from which the paper derives its research-driven guidelines for educators on promoting student responsibility for learning.
requirements: The model presupposes PBL settings in which students carry responsibility for the learning process from project start to end
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students engaged in problem- or project-based learning
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills such as goal setting, monitoring, reflection, and motivation maintenance
examples: The paper uses the model to organize research-driven guidelines on how to promote student responsibility for learning in PBL.

article_title: Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review
citation: Sofie M. M. Loyens, Julianne E. van Meerten, Lydia Schaap, Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09757-x
title: Barrows' six core characteristics and three-phase process model of problem-based learning
description: The review characterizes PBL through Barrows' (1996) six core characteristics — student-centered learning, small groups with a tutor, the tutor as facilitator, authentic problems encountered before study, problems as triggers for prior knowledge activation revealing knowledge gaps, and self-directed learning to close those gaps. It adds that "PBL as a process consists of three separate stages: an initial discussion phase, a self-study phase, and a reporting stage." These criteria also served as inclusion criteria for judging whether studies genuinely implemented PBL.
requirements: Implementation must include authentic problems as the start of learning, collaborative small groups, a facilitating tutor, and ample time for self-directed self-study
constraints: Studies whose learning process started with a lecture instead of a problem, or that did not contain the three process phases, were excluded as not meeting the defining criteria
target_learning_goals: Domain knowledge acquisition through self-directed learning on authentic problems
examples: The review's inclusion coding assessed studies' definitions and implementations against these characteristics (Barrows, 1996; Hmelo-Silver, 2004; Schmidt et al., 2009)

article_title: CGRP inhibition in the PBN shifts defensive strategy from freezing to active avoidance in a platform-based active avoidance paradigm
citation: Hanny Hayeon Lee, Eul Han & Yong Sang Jo. (2026). CGRP inhibition in the PBN shifts defensive strategy from freezing to active avoidance in a platform-based active avoidance paradigm. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00453-3
title: Platform-based active avoidance (PBA) paradigm
description: The PBA paradigm is an operant defensive-learning task in which an auditory tone CS predicts a footshock US and mice avoid shock by moving onto a central platform safe zone within the first 5 s of CS onset. The authors developed it because it "eliminates appetitive reinforcement", letting animals learn "to avoid shock by moving onto a permanently available platform without any competing reward demands", thereby isolating threat-driven avoidance and defensive response selection from food-motivation confounds.
requirements: A permanent safe zone (8 × 8 cm platform) continuously available in the operant chamber; an auditory CS (12 kHz, 50 dB) coterminating with a footshock US; trial-by-trial scoring of platform entry within the first 5 s of CS onset by an experimenter blind to shock intensity and group.
constraints: Continuous platform availability produces stay behaviour (conditioning stay rate: 46%; retention test stay rate: 15%), so passive occupancy must be separated from cue-evoked entries when interpreting avoidance learning.
target_learners: mice (CalcaCre/+ and C57BL/6J, approximately 3-6 months old)
target_learning_goals: defensive response selection between passive and active strategies
examples: Independent cohorts were conditioned at 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 or 0.5 mA across four days alternating afternoon conditioning sessions (25 CS-US trials) with next-day CS-only retention tests (4 CS presentations).

article_title: Effectiveness of Problem-Based Learning on Secondary Students' Achievement in Science: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Funa, A. A., & Prudente, M. S. (2021). Effectiveness of problem-based learning on secondary students’ achievement in science: A meta-analysis. International Journal of Instruction, 14(4), 69-84. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.1445a
title: PBL implementations in secondary science most commonly combine collaboration, probing questions, student choice of solution path, and essay-form problem solving
description: Across the 11 pooled studies, the article identifies the recurring instructional configuration of PBL in secondary science: collaboration among students, probing questions during lecture, freedom to choose how to solve the problem, and qualitative problem solving in essay form. The article reports these "strategies were included in the core elements of incorporating PBL in teaching", while quantitative problem solving, reflection, concept cartoon integration, and mind mapping were least used. ICT, multimedia, and graphic organizers were integrated during lectures and presentation of investigation results.
requirements: Problems must be at the heart of the instructional material and drive students’ curiosity and learning, per the article’s definition of PBL
constraints: The reflexive part of PBL (self-assessment and collaborative reflection) was not emphasized by the analyzed studies, which the authors attribute to the quasi-experimental designs focused on quantitative effectiveness
examples: All 11 studies (100%) used collaboration, probing questions during lecture, and choice on how to solve the problem; 91% used qualitative problem solving in essay form (Table 6).

citation: Funa, A. A., & Prudente, M. S. (2021). Effectiveness of problem-based learning on secondary students’ achievement in science: A meta-analysis. International Journal of Instruction, 14(4), 69-84. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.1445a
title: Use PBL as a supplemental approach with the teacher acting as guide, tutor, and facilitator
description: Based on the meta-analytic finding that PBL produces a large positive effect on secondary science achievement, the article recommends that "PBL be used as a supplemental approach to the existing teaching methods and strategies in science". It further states that "the presence of teacher as guide, tutor, and facilitator is integral" when applying PBL in science teaching, and that teachers may combine different teaching strategies with PBL to target particular skills. The article also recommends developing teachers’ skills in delivering PBL approaches.
requirements: The presence of the teacher as guide, tutor, and facilitator during PBL application
Teachers’ understanding that students learn in different ways
constraints: PBL has limitations that may hinder meaningful utilization, most especially its application in enhancing academic performance of younger students, per the article’s conclusion
examples: The article recommends future studies venture into teachers’ capacity to implement PBL in their classes and integration of PBL with newly emerged innovative teaching strategies.

article_title: The Effect of Problem-Based Learning in Science Education on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analytical Study
citation: Ufuk Uluçınar. (2022). The Effect of Problem-Based Learning in Science Education on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analytical Study. Science Education International, 34(2), 72-85. https://doi.org/10.33828/sei.v34.i2.1
title: Problem-based learning as a constructivist, student-centered instructional model structured around ill-structured authentic problems
description: PBL is described as "a student-centered, active learning approach" in which students construct knowledge "through peer interaction and collaborative research or inquiry". Its essential component is an ill-structured authentic real-life problem scenario, and a PBL sequence consists of seven stages, from clarifying terms and defining the problem through constructing learning objectives to integrating and controlling newly acquired knowledge. The teacher facilitates rather than presents information, helping students learn cognitive skills for problem-solving and collaboration. This meta-analysis treats PBL as the independent variable and science academic achievement as the dependent variable.
requirements: An ill-structured authentic real-life problem scenario as the essential component of learning
Teacher facilitation of cognitive and collaboration skills instead of presenting information

citation: Clemens Megan, Boparai Josheil Kaur, Dawe Russell, Avery Susan. (2026). Problem-based and related learning approaches in family medicine residency: a scoping review of four countries. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.81284
title: Three categories of synchronous PBL delivery in family medicine residency curricula: standalone, adjunct, and blended
description: The review organizes how the 12 included studies integrated PBL into family medicine postgraduate curricula into three synchronous delivery categories. As the authors state, "We found three distinct categories of synchronous approaches to integrating PBL into family medicine PGME curricula: 1) standalone, 2) adjunct, and 3) blended." Standalone approaches use PBL as the primary instructional mode; adjunct approaches add PBL sessions to traditional lecture-based delivery; blended approaches integrate PBL within established curriculum methods such as rotations, conferences, and engaged-classroom sessions.
requirements: Synchronous delivery involving multiple learners, since real-time interaction and problem-solving are described as essential features of PBL
constraints: The taxonomy applies to synchronous formats only; asynchronous environments were excluded from the review
target_learning_goals: application of learning to clinical practice
examples: Klein et al. paired a large-group lecture academic half-day with a small-group PBL session on the same topic the following month, an adjunct approach

title: Successful PBL implementation in residency depends on resident buy-in, protected time, and faculty preparedness
description: Across the 12 included studies, the review identifies enabling conditions for implementing PBL in family medicine residency curricula. In its conclusion the authors state that "Successful implementation depended on resident buy-in, protected time, and faculty preparedness." The pattern spans the three delivery categories (standalone, adjunct, blended), all of which used synchronous small-group formats in which learners addressed clinical problems and synthesized solutions. The review also notes faculty observers valued PBL and learners generally participated equally, fostering collaboration.

protected time for learners
faculty preparedness, including facilitation capability

citation: Fernandes Ivan Filho; Rodrigues Cibele Isaac Saad; Korkes Henri Augusto; de Sampaio Luiz Ferraz Neto. (2025). Problem-based learning in obstetrics and gynecology: a systematic review. Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia e Obstetrícia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12711243/
title: PBL tutorial structure: small groups with Maastricht seven-step sessions and facilitator role
description: The article describes PBL sessions as "small groups with about eight to ten students and one facilitating professor". Through two sessions, students discuss scenarios ruled by the Maastricht seven steps: a first session where a secretary and coordinator are chosen, individual self-study, then a second session where participants discuss the results of each student's individual studies. The facilitating professor oversees the process, ensuring students stay on topic and providing guidance when needed.
requirements: Small groups of about eight to ten students with one facilitating professor
Two structured sessions following the Maastricht seven steps, with individual self-study between them
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in obstetrics and gynecology

citation: Abugri Bruce Ayabilla, Assibi Maxwell Ateni, Amalba Anthony, Gaa Patience Kanyiri, Kpebu Sophia E.A., Karikari Patience Afua Adwaapa, Mogre Victor. (2026). The effects of problem-based learning (PBL) on undergraduate medical students' critical thinking and communication skills development: A scoping review across resource-rich and resource-limited settings (2015-2024). PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342599
title: Working definition of problem-based learning as a student-centred, facilitated small-group tutorial cycle organised by an authentic problem trigger
description: The review defines PBL as "a student-centred approach delivered through facilitated small-group tutorials in which an authentic problem scenario (the trigger) is presented first and serves as the main organiser of learning". Students analyse the trigger, identify learning needs, formulate objectives, complete self-directed study, and reconvene to integrate and apply new knowledge, with the tutor facilitating process rather than delivering content. What distinguishes PBL is that students generate the learning agenda from the problem and use a structured tutorial cycle; in case-based learning cases more often support consolidation of already-taught content, while inquiry-based learning may not use a problem trigger as the central organiser.
requirements: A tutor who facilitates process and discussion rather than delivers content
constraints: Distinguished from case-based learning and inquiry-based learning by the problem trigger as central curriculum organiser and the structured tutorial cycle

citation: Chen Tu, Zhao Yi-Jing, Huang Feng-Qing, Liu Qun, Li Ying, Alolga Raphael N., Zhang Lei, Ma Gaoxiang. (2024). PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0314017
title: Problem-based learning as a seven-step, student-centered, problem-driven instructional process
description: The article describes PBL as "a student-centered learning strategy that uses a problem as a starting point to facilitate learning", in which pharmacy students collaborate in small groups to improve cognitive capacities and clinical and critical thinking skills. It enumerates seven steps: identifying the problem, exploring prior knowledge, generating potential theories, identifying learning needs, individually gathering research, re-evaluating and applying new knowledge, and reflecting on the learning process. In this study PBL was implemented in the Authentication of Chinese Medicines course, an applied discipline on identifying and studying varieties and quality of Chinese medicines.
requirements: A problem used as the starting point for learning and small-group collaboration of students
constraints: The article's evidence base is pharmacy students in a Chinese pharmaceutical university course; the meta-analysis included only English and Chinese language articles
examples: The 17-week Authentication of Chinese Medicines course at China Pharmaceutical University was delivered in PBL format with about two hours a week, compared against lecture-based learning.

article_title: Use of problem-based learning in orthopaedics education: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Li Ting, Song Ruohong, Zhong Wenjie, Liao Wenao, Hu Jiang, Liu Xilin, Wang Fei. (2024). Use of problem-based learning in orthopaedics education: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05244-1
title: Adopt PBL in orthopaedics clinical teaching while planning for added study time demands and pressure
description: The review concludes that the PBL teaching model can significantly improve the quality of clinical teaching and is worth promoting and applying, because pooled results favour PBL on knowledge, skills, satisfaction and process abilities. At the same time it reports that students can feel higher levels of study pressure and experience less study time, so adoption should be paired with provision of learning space, time, and resources. The authors state the findings need to be further verified in multicentre, double-blind and large-sample RCTs.
requirements: PBL requires a high level of self-directed learning and collaboration skills from students
providing students with more learning space, time, and resources to support self-study and group discussions
constraints: all included studies were from China, and some pooled results were strongly subjective
only English and Chinese studies were included, which may have led to language bias and heterogeneity
half of the included studies did not provide detailed information on the frequency and duration of PBL interventions
risk of bias increased due to lack of information about randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding of outcome assessment in some studies
target_learning_goals: problem-solving, independent learning, teamwork, communication and clinical reasoning abilities
examples: The review pooled 51 RCTs (4268 patients) comparing PBL with lecture-based learning across orthopaedics teaching topics such as basic theory, imageology, arthroscopy training and failure-case analysis.

title: PBL's three main learning objectives: deep content learning, problem analysis and solution development, and self-directed learning
description: The article frames problem-based learning as an approach in which students "learn actively using case-based peer-to-peer teaching" under a facilitator's guidance, aiming to integrate learned knowledge rather than implant it. It names "three main learning objectives": applying deep content learning, applying problem analysis skills to develop solutions, and applying self-directed learning to adapt learning styles. This framework organizes the three outcome domains the meta-analysis evaluates.
requirements: Implementation requires students to formulate their own learning goals from PBL scenarios, solve problems via literature and internet, and actively participate in group discussions under facilitator guidance
constraints: The article notes students familiar with teacher-centered methods tend to face difficulty applying the student-centered PBL method in higher education
examples: The meta-analysis evaluated each of the three objectives as a separate pooled outcome across the seven included studies

article_title: The Effect of Problem-Based Learning on Improvement of the Medical Educational Environment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Qin Yongjie, Wang Yungui, Floden Robert E. (2016). The Effect of Problem-Based Learning on Improvement of the Medical Educational Environment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Medical Principles and Practice. https://doi.org/10.1159/000449036
title: PBL small-group tutorial structure with facilitator tutor and five-step process
description: The article describes problem-based learning as "a nontraditional, active, inductive, student-centered approach to learning" that develops self-learning, collaboration, problem solving and critical thinking. Its distinguishing feature is small tutorial groups of 6–8 students with a tutor acting as facilitator or guide rather than expert or purveyor of knowledge. The PBL process follows five basic steps: problem analysis, establishment of learning objectives, collection of information, summarizing, and reflection. In the included trials, PBL was implemented in groups of 4–6 students with mentors or 15-student groups with scenarios.
requirements: Small tutorial groups with a tutor facilitating rather than lecturing
A problem or scenario as the trigger for learning
constraints: Contrasted throughout with traditional lecture-based learning characterized by large class sizes and instructor-driven delivery
examples: In one included study, PBL groups of 4–6 students with one mentor followed a PBL process with one scenario every 2 weeks over 3 months

article_title: Effects of problem-based learning in Chinese radiology education: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Zhang Song, Xu Jiancheng, Wang Hongwei, Zhang Dong, Zhang Qichuan, Zou Liguang. (2018). Effects of problem-based learning in Chinese radiology education: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000010069
title: Problem-based learning as a student-centered approach organized around four key principles
description: The article describes PBL as a student-centered teaching approach introduced by Barrows and Tamblyn at McMaster University, with "4 key principles of PBL, including contextual learning, information processing, cooperative learning, and self-determination." In radiology it places imaging in a clinical context, with students learning through practice in a tutor-guided small group around organ-system-based scenarios, contrasting with passive lecture-based learning.
requirements: PBL scenarios based on organ systems suit radiology's subspecialization
tutor-guided small groups with clinical scenarios
constraints: In China, application lags behind developed countries due to curricula arrangement, large classes, deficiency of tutors, and high tuition fees
target_learners: medical students in Chinese medical universities or colleges

citation: Liu CX, Ouyang WW, Wang XW, Chen D, Jiang ZL. (2020). Comparing hybrid problem-based and lecture learning (PBL + LBL) with LBL pedagogy on clinical curriculum learning for medical students in China: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000019687
title: Use PBL as a supplement to LBL rather than replacing lecturing, to combine systematic knowledge delivery with problem-based engagement
description: The article advocates hybrid PBL+LBL, in which "PBL as a supplement to the application of the LBL pedagogy alone in a clinical curriculum". The rationale is that LBL alone limits active thinking while PBL alone may leave gaps in systematicness and depth within limited teaching hours; the hybrid lets students master knowledge points systematically while training problem-solving through case- and problem-based guidance. The authors conclude it "can be advocated and popularized as teaching means".
requirements: PBL problems and courses require adequate design, since the article notes insufficient design of PBL problems as a problem in practice
Teaching units should improve standards, teaching materials, question banks and teachers for PBL+LBL teaching
constraints: Evidence comes from Chinese medical students in specialized clinical curricula; the authors note the conclusion may lack representativeness globally and that not all clinical curricula were covered
target_learners: clinical medicine students, particularly those in the transition to clinical years
target_learning_goals: clinical thinking skills, basic clinical skills, doctor-patient communication, diagnostic and problem-solving ability
examples: The 20 included trials all implemented PBL+LBL as the experimental arm against an LBL-only control across specialized clinical courses

title: Problem-based learning as an educational method for pharmacy education
description: Problem-based learning (PBL) is an educational method focused on self-directed learning, small group discussion with facilitators, and working through problems to acquire knowledge. In a PBL course, the instructor helps students develop problem solving skills, self-directed learning, collaboration skills and intrinsic motivation, leading students to identify what they know, what they need to know, and how and where to access new information. The review applies this method to pharmacy education, where students learn by working with real-life cases.
requirements: Small group discussion of cases led by a facilitator
Working through problems to acquire knowledge
constraints: The review notes the main barriers for implementing PBL are teacher and staff training and a necessary reduction in class size
examples: Included studies used small group discussion of cases led by a facilitator, with or without problem solving, across externship, clerkship, and continuing education contexts

title: PBL teaching model as defined by Kinkade: small-group, case-based learning with hypotheses and out-of-class objectives
description: The article adopts Kinkade's definition of the PBL teaching model as "a curriculum of carefully selected activities that test the learner's critical knowledge acquisition, problem-solving, self-directed learning, and team-participation capacities." Students work in small groups, generate hypotheses about a given case and learning objectives, work outside of class hours to fulfill learning objectives, and then reconvene and solve the problem. In the reviewed studies, PBL was applied for one semester in experimental groups, either alone or combined with LBL, with teachers facilitating student learning through experimentation, clinical cases, and seminars.
requirements: Small-group student work with case materials and learning objectives
Out-of-class work to fulfill learning objectives before reconvening to solve the problem

citation: Zhou Jiyin, Zhou Shiwen, Huang Chunji, Xu Rufu, Zhang Zuo, Zeng Shengya, Qian Guisheng. (2016). Effectiveness of problem-based learning in Chinese pharmacy education: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0546-z
title: Adopt PBL as an optional, supplementary teaching method in Chinese pharmacy education, tailored to local institutional needs
description: The article concludes that PBL pedagogy, shown to outperform lecture-based teaching in pooled Chinese pharmacy trials, should be adopted incrementally rather than as wholesale replacement. It states "PBL methods could be an optional, supplementary method of pharmaceutical teaching in China", and that institutions "should revise PBL curricula according to their own needs, which would maximize the effectiveness of PBL". This positions PBL as a context-sensitive addition to existing pharmacy curricula, not a one-size-fits-all mandate.
requirements: Institutional capacity for smaller tutorial groups and teacher training, since the article notes main obstacles include training of teachers and staff and necessary decreases in class size
constraints: Chinese pharmacy education has special teaching conditions (limited equipment, varied institutional standards, traditional teacher-oriented methods) making direct imitation of foreign PBL models difficult
target_learners: Undergraduate pharmacy students in Chinese colleges and universities
target_learning_goals: Professional reasoning and self-directed learning skills
examples: The 16 included trials implemented PBL across disciplines such as pharmaceutical analysis, natural medicine chemistry, and biopharmaceutics, each with tutorial groups of roughly 4–22 students over one or two semesters

description: The article frames PBL's advantage through an active-engagement mechanism: "Learning is most effective when students are actively involved in PBL". The authors also note PBL "encourages students to think about and resolve practical problems" and may help students apply knowledge to work situations, improve professional reasoning, and encourage self-directed learning during professional careers.

Problem-centered curriculum design rather than factual-knowledge dissemination
constraints: The article presents this as the authors' interpretation of why PBL outperformed lectures, not as a directly tested mechanism in the included trials

target_learning_goals: Application of knowledge to practical work situations

A tutor-led small group in which students learn through problem solving

About one month for students to prepare projects
Heterogeneous groups of about three students with end-of-term presentations
constraints: Evidence comes from one quasi-experimental study with two 8th-grade classes in a single urban middle school in Trabzon; students were not randomly assigned
target_learning_goals: Positive attitudes towards statistics, statistical literacy

article_title: Project Based Learning: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Menzies, V., Hewitt, C., Kokotsaki, D., Collyer, C. and Wiggins, A. (2016). Project Based Learning: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/public/files/Projects/EEF_Project_Protocol_ProjectBasedLearning.pdf
title: Project based learning as constructivist, student-centred inquiry culminating in a concrete artefact
description: The report's literature review frames project based learning as "a student-centred form of instruction based on three constructivist principles": learning is context-specific, learners are actively involved, and goals are achieved through social interaction and shared knowledge. It is treated as a particular type of inquiry-based learning in which authentic real-world questions provide the context, and its distinctiveness lies in "the construction of an end product, a ‘concrete artefact’" representing pupils' new understanding, often presented via videos, reports, models and other artefacts. The review attributes this framing to cited authors such as Cocco (2006) and Helle et al. (2006).
requirements: Authentic questions and problems within real-world practices to provide the learning context
Active learner involvement and social interaction and knowledge sharing
constraints: The review notes the existing causal evidence for PBL effects on attainment is weak, with most studies non-randomised
examples: The review cites Al-Balushi and Al-Aamri (2014) on environmental science projects and Hernández-Ramos and De La Paz (2009) on multimedia mini-documentaries in history as instances of this inquiry-with-artefact framing.

citation: Fateme Shir Mohammadi. (2017). The Effect of Authentic Problem-Based Vocabulary Tasks on Vocabulary Learning of EFL Learners. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 5(3). https://www.ijels.aiac.org.au
title: Problem-based learning as a constructivist, real-life approach using cognitive and metacognitive skills
description: The article frames PBL as "a collaborative, self-directed approach to learning which makes use of language learners' cognitive and metacognitive thinking skills". It treats PBL as constructivist, seeking answers to problems as perceived by learners, with no fixed correct answers in tutorship. PBL tasks aim at mimicking real-life problems so that learning resembles learners' real-life problems, and the approach views learning as analyzing and decoding content rather than memorizing it.
requirements: Problems designed for learners must be authentic and resemble real-life problems
constraints: The article notes the way PBL can be implemented is not fixed, which it says has led to misconceptions and misapplication of the approach
examples: The study implemented PBL in vocabulary classes using real-life scenarios such as a dripping tap learners must resolve with their landlord

article_title: Learning Physics through Project-Based Learning Game Techniques
citation: Baran, M., Maskan, A., & Yaşar, Ş. (2018). Learning Physics through Project-Based Learning Game Techniques. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 221-234. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11215a
title: Project-based learning game technique: students design and present physical game tools embodying physics laws
description: This pattern combines project-based learning with game techniques: student groups design physical game tools that embody target physics concepts, build them over several weeks, and present and explain the physics to classmates. In the study, participants "were divided into 7 groups and asked to design game tool projects appropriate for the assigned topics" covering Newton's Laws of Motion, producing projects such as a rocket car, swing, dominos, slide, bumper carts, carousel, billiard, bowling balls with Newton's cradle, golf, ball spinning, and arrow. In the fifth week students presented the game systems to their classmates.
requirements: Students work in groups on assigned physics topics
A presentation phase in which students explain the physics of their game tools to classmates
A multi-week classroom period for designing and building the game tools
constraints: Students had difficulties finding necessary materials, so the article recommends providing needed equipment and appropriate infrastructure before implementation
Presentation was the most challenging phase for students due to anxiety
target_learning_goals: Understanding Newton's Laws of Motion (inertia, action-reaction, friction, second law)
examples: Over four weeks students designed game tools based on Newton's Laws of Motion in the classroom setting, then presented them in the fifth week; projects included a slide illustrating the Law of Friction and a carousel illustrating the Law of Inertia.

article_title: Does Problem-Based Learning Improve Problem Solving Skills?--A Study among Business Undergraduates at Malaysian Premier Technical University
citation: Z. Abdul Kadir, N. H. Abdullah, E. Anthony, B. Mohd Salleh & R. Kamarulzaman. (2016). description: In its discussion, the article frames why PBL works via a process account: the problem-solving process "was guided by a framework where students learn to explore and analyse problems systematically (Dochy et al., 2005)", making students proactive and expanding existing knowledge bases. constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation of prior literature, not a tested mechanism in this study
examples: Students given a trigger by the lecturer-facilitator gather information via library research and the Internet, conduct meetings, interact with people, and prepare presentations

citation: Balım, A. G., İnel-Ekici, D., & Özcan, E. (2016). Concept Cartoons Supported Problem Based Learning Method in Middle School Science Classrooms. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n2p272
title: Problem based learning as student-centred, small-group learning from semi-structured daily-life problems
description: The article characterises problem based learning as a student-centred method that begins when students must solve a semi-structured problem taken from daily life, works in small groups of 6-8 students, and requires self-directed learning with high-end thinking skills such as research, critical thinking and inquiry. Because it demands high-end thinking, the article notes it is generally used in high schools and universities, motivating visual supports like concept cartoons for lower secondary use.

small cooperative groups of 6-8 students
teacher-leaders who supervise and guide rather than explain

citation: Tatag Yuli Eko SISWONO, Sugi HARTONO, Ahmad Wachidul KOHAR. (2018). Effectiveness of Project Based Learning in Statistics for Lower Secondary Schools. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 75, 197-212.
title: Six-aspect project-based learning design combining authentic challenges, active exploration, and formal and informal assessment

article_title: The Effect of Project Based Learning on Seventh Grade Students' Academic Achievement
citation: Kızkapan, O. & Bektaş, O. (2017). The Effect of Project Based Learning on Seventh Grade Students' Academic Achievement. International Journal of Instruction, 10(1), 37-54. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_1_3.pdf
title: Project-based learning as a constructivist science teaching strategy
description: The article frames PBL as one of the constructivist teaching strategies used in science classes, in which learners construct and interpret new knowledge rather than memorize. title: Problem Based Economics unit structure: seven interrelated problem-solving phases with a facilitative teacher
description: Each PBE unit contains "seven interrelated phases: entry, problem framing, knowledge inventory, problem research and resources, problem twist, problem log, problem exit, and problem debriefing." The teacher takes a facilitative role, answering questions, moving groups along, and waiting for teachable moments before intervening or providing content explanations, so students do not learn entirely on their own but the timing and extent of interventions differ from traditional approaches.
requirements: A case-study module well-suited to student-driven problem solving
Teacher facilitation with interventions timed to teachable moments rather than continuous direct instruction
constraints: The phases scaffold and, to some degree, constrain teacher and student behavior; units can take from one day to three weeks to complete
target_learning_goals: Contextualizing, understanding, reasoning about, and solving economic problems
examples: In a consistent implementation an observer might see students confronting a real-world dilemma allowing more than one solution, seeking needed knowledge, and being motivated to learn standards-based content

title: Problem-based learning as a learner-centered approach with five goals: flexible knowledge, problem-solving, self-directed learning, collaboration, and intrinsic motivation
description: The article presents PBL as a learner-centered method in which "the PBL teacher is a facilitator of student learning", carried out in small groups through discussion, problem solving, and study with peers. Citing Barrows and Kelson (1995), it lists five aims: constructing an extensive and flexible knowledge base; developing effective problem-solving skills; developing self-directed, lifelong learning skills; becoming effective collaborators; and becoming intrinsically motivated to learn. The study applies this framework to EFL speaking through cognition-based tasks.
requirements: A facilitator who scaffolds through modeling and questioning strategies, with scaffolding decreasing as students become more experienced with PBL
Small-group structure in which learners divide learning issues and collaborate
constraints: The article notes there is not yet evidence that PBL helps students become better collaborators broadly defined, and little research bears directly on intrinsic motivation
target_learners: professional and higher-education students in medical and other disciplines as reviewed
examples: The study operationalized PBL in twenty sessions using modified course materials with problem-scenarios replacing conversations

title: PBL tutorial cycle: minimal-information problem presentation, learner questioning, and reflection at completion
description: The article describes the PBL learning cycle as "enacted through the tutorial process that begins with the presentation of a problem and ends with student reflection". A session begins by presenting a group of students with minimal information about a complex problem; students must question the facilitator to obtain additional information and may gather facts through experiments or research. When completing the problem, students reflect on what they learned, how well they cooperated, and how effectively they directed their learning.
requirements: A tutor who aids learners only after they have used sources at their disposal, including their own cognition, peers' help, and online and paperback sources
Problems made implicit enough that they cannot be decoded from the description alone, a change made after piloting
constraints: For less uniformly skilled learners, the article reports direct instruction is needed and varying kinds of scaffolding might be needed
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners in small tutorial groups
examples: The researcher piloted the procedure in 4 sessions and revised problem implicitness and tutor-help timing before the main study

citation: Alfred Olufemi Fatade, David Mogari, Abayomi Adelaja Arigbabu. (2013). EFFECT OF PROBLEM-BASED LEARNING ON SENIOR SECONDARY SCHOOL STUDENTS’ ACHIEVEMENTS IN FURTHER MATHEMATICS. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 6, Number 3. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/2065-1430
title: A five-phase problem-solving process enacted in heterogeneous learners' community groups structures PBL for secondary mathematics lessons
description: The article's PBL implementation organised each lesson around a flowchart of problem processes and grouped students heterogeneously. As printed, "the PBL group process adopted consisted of five phases namely (i) identify the problem (ii) make assumptions (iii) formulate a model (iv) use the model and (v) evaluate the model." The 42 experimental students formed six groups of seven, seated semi-circularly so the teacher could walk across groups, with group members presenting solutions and peers critiquing them while the teacher acted as facilitator.
requirements: Students grouped heterogeneously by prior performance; seating arranged so the facilitator can move between groups; ill-structured tasks with multiple solutions; teacher orientation on PBL before implementation
constraints: The rigid school timetable allowed only two 40-minute periods per week and no extension of classroom activities beyond closing time
target_learners: Senior Secondary School year one Further Mathematics students (mean age about 15 years)
target_learning_goals: Indices and logarithms, algebraic equations, sequences and series; problem solving and conceptual understanding in Further Mathematics
examples: In the first PBL period students investigated the correctness of given index equations individually and in groups; one member each from the first three groups presented on the chalkboard while other members critiqued, triggering classroom dialogue resolved by teacher-facilitated simplification of both sides of the equation

title: Use PBL instead of lecture-based instruction in computer courses for pre-service teachers to promote active participation and meaningful learning
description: The article concludes that lecture-based computer courses are inadequate for actively engaging pre-service teachers in constructing effective and meaningful learning, and recommends PBL approaches instead. It states that "providing active participation in the learning process is not possible by solely providing pre -service teachers with lecturer examples on computers" and that lecturers should present problems with different structures than those demonstrated in class.

Small student groups of five to nine members (the study used groups of six or seven)
constraints: Findings are limited to MS Excel functions in a basic computer course
Evaluation was based on an achievement test with open-ended questions

meaningful and deep learning of computer course content
examples: In the study, PBL group participants worked on real-life problem situations in small groups of six or seven members over seven weeks, while LBCC participants received lectures and individually practiced sample exercises on computers.

description: The article describes a reusable weekly PBL cycle for computer courses: the lecturer presents a problem situation at the beginning of class, small groups spend two course hours drafting a problem-solving plan, groups meet during the week to develop solutions, and at week's end each group projects their solutions to other groups and submits a problem report. This cycle was implemented over seven weeks with groups of six or seven members.

title: Six characteristics of problem-based learning
description: The article describes six PBL characteristics drawn from Barrows (1994, 1996), Gijbels et al. (2005), and Reynolds and Hancock (2010): (1) learning is student-centered, (2) learning occurs in small student groups of five to nine members, (3) teachers act as facilitators or student guides, (4) problems form the organizing focus and stimulus for learning, (5) problems are vehicles for the development of problem-solving skills, and (6) new information is acquired through self-directed learning. The article situates PBL within constructivism, noting it is compatible with Dewey's empiricism and Bruner's discovery learning.
requirements: Small student groups of five to nine members
Teachers acting as facilitators rather than lecturers
Real-life problem situations presented in various formats
constraints: Originally developed for medical education at McMaster University in the late 1960s
examples: Problems can be presented to students as written papers, computer simulations, video or audio recorders.

title: Use PBL to cultivate critical thinking in English teaching because it centres students on real problem situations
description: The article recommends the PBL teaching model for English courses because it takes students as the centre and provides "students with the real problem situation", asking them to analyse problems and construct new knowledge in small teams. The 12-week experiment showed gains in selected critical thinking temperaments and skills, supporting its use for critical thinking cultivation rather than score improvement.

title: PBL teaching model as a constructivist, five-step problem-centred teaching organization
description: The article describes the PBL teaching model as problem-based learning grounded in constructivist teaching theory. It "takes the students as the center, provides students with the real problem situation", has students analyse problems, identify relevant facts, and construct new knowledge and solve problems in small teams. The model is divided into five major steps: "question-analysis-problem solving-results reporting-reflection and evaluation", and bears features of autonomy, openness and cooperation.

citation: Ajai, J.T. & Imoko, I.I. (2015). Gender differences in mathematics achievement and retention scores: A case of problem-based learning method. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(1), 45-50. http://www.ijres.net
title: Problem-based learning as facilitated, small-group, self-directed exploration of problems
description: The article describes PBL as "a range of pedagogical approaches that encourage students to learn through the structured exploration of a research problem." Class activities are built around problems rather than lectures; students take the initiative to inquire, apply what they learn back to the problem, and become responsible for their own learning, while the teacher acts as a facilitator whose interventions diminish over time. The method is characteristically carried out in small facilitated groups that exploit the social aspect of learning through discussion, problem solving, and peer study, forming what the authors call a cognitive apprenticeship.

constraints: The study reports this as a case study of algebra instruction in Benue State, Nigeria

examples: Students were taught topics in change of subject formulae, substitution, variations, factorization and quadratic equations over four weeks using PBL lessons based on the SS2 mathematics curriculum

title: Combined PBL-CBL model integrating structured clinical cases with inquiry-based problem-solving
description: The article describes a hybrid pedagogy that "combin[es] the structured clinical context of CBL with the inquiry-based, student-driven nature of PBL". title: Position a time-limited PBL bridge course at the basic-clinical interface as a low-disruption alternative to full curriculum restructuring.
description: The article presents a 36-hour integrated PBL bridge course strategically positioned in the fifth semester, after core basic sciences and before clinical clerkships, as a "targeted, plug-in solution at the basic-clinical interface". This design preserves the existing discipline-based curriculum rather than requiring the full restructuring demanded by organ-system integration models, making it suitable for institutions where full-scale curriculum reform is not feasible due to resource constraints or regulatory requirements.

A dedicated teaching team with tutors experienced in PBL pedagogy
constraints: The evaluation design lacked a control group, precluding causal claims about superiority over other instructional methods
Findings are based on student perceptions and process-oriented performance data rather than objective measures of clinical competence

examples: The course was implemented as a mandatory 36-contact-hour component in the fifth semester that did not replace any existing courses in the discipline-based curriculum.

title: 16-item Process Evaluation Rubric combining self-assessment (20%), peer assessment (20%), and tutor assessment (60%) across four domains.

title: Social constructivism as the primary theoretical framework for the integrated PBL bridge course, supplemented by cognitive load theory and situated learning theory.
description: The article grounds the course design in social constructivism, positing that "knowledge is actively constructed by learners through social interaction, dialogue, and collaborative problem solving—processes that are central to PBL tutorials." The PBL tutorial's collaborative case discussion creates a "zone of proximal development" in which learners co-construct knowledge with scaffolding from peers and tutors. Cognitive load theory informs the progressive release of case information across the three-session cycle, while situated learning theory grounds learning in authentic clinical contexts aligned with cognitive apprenticeship.
requirements: Small-group tutorials that create a social context for learners to activate prior knowledge and collectively construct new knowledge
Tutor facilitation that guides rather than directs discussion
target_learning_goals: Integration of basic science knowledge into clinical reasoning frameworks
examples: The structured cases function as 'worked examples' that demonstrate hypothesis-driven reasoning pathways, a strategy theorized to reduce extraneous load and foster transferable knowledge structures.

description: A two-step instructional element replacing a lecture on Immunity to COVID-19: groups of ten created domain-specific mind maps from assigned research articles, then integrated them into a class-wide conceptual framework. Small-group division with instructor guidance and templates as initial structured support

article_title: Bereavement practices and staff competencies on perinatal loss at a community-based teaching hospital.
citation: Garavito C, Karki S, Rose SJ, Hartnett J. (2026). Bereavement practices and staff competencies on perinatal loss at a community-based teaching hospital. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0347348
title: Perinatal Bereavement Care Confidence Scale (PBCCS), modified to 32 items for U.S. acute-care staff
description: The PBCCS is a validated questionnaire developed by the Australian College of Midwives to measure factors affecting bereavement support provision; its internal consistency "ranges from 0.753 to 0.871". The study team adapted the original 43-item tool for U.S. acute-care hospital staff, removing 14 questions and adding three organizational-support items, producing a 32-item instrument with subscales for knowledge, skills, self-awareness, and organizational support, scored 1–5 per item with a total range of 32–160 and 80% (128) as sufficient confidence.
requirements: Permission was requested from and granted by the instrument's developers; items are rated on a 1–5 Likert scale and the total is computed from subscale mean scores
constraints: The validity and reliability of the modified 32-item version were not re-evaluated; the tool was originally developed for midwives and nurses in Ireland rather than U.S. acute-care hospital staff
Respondents missing item data were excluded per-item without imputation, so denominators vary across items
target_learners: Hospital staff in Maternity, Labor and Delivery, and Emergency Departments
target_learning_goals: Bereavement care confidence: knowledge, skills, self-awareness, and organizational support for perinatal loss care
examples: Used as the dependent variable in a cross-sectional needs-assessment survey of 46 staff, with results reported by subscale, department, and formal-education status

description: A lesson-level instructional pattern combining flipped pre-class preparation with problem-based small-group inquiry. One week before class, teams receive texts, PPT slides, e-books, videos and online platform resources and investigate topics "aligned with current social issues in China" such as fireworks-related ocular injuries. description: The article describes a combined model in which problem-based learning and case-based learning are used together so that, in the authors' words, "PBL improving students' subjective initiative and CBL enhancing students' collaborative ability and understanding of clinical knowledge". A teacher-to-student ratio of 1:10 as used in this study

citation: Li Heyu, Lu Yang, Tian Yang, Zhou Li, Wang Danna. (2025). Mechanism of an integrated PBL-KAP-AI spiral health education model for breast cancer patients. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1687956
title: PBL-KAP-AI spiral health education model
description: The model integrates Problem-Based Learning, the Knowledge–Attitude–Practice framework, and AI-driven dynamic feedback into a closed-loop iterative process of "PBL-guided—KAP-deepened—AI-feedback". Unlike traditional linear health education models, its core is a nonlinear iterative process in which patients undergo multiple educational cycles, each encompassing PBL-guided learning, KAP-based knowledge and belief deepening, and dynamic AI feedback. Iteration initiation is determined by AI's assessment of learning progress, health behavior, and emotional state rather than fixed time points. The model was tested in a randomized trial with breast cancer patients.
requirements: Requires an AI platform analyzing clinical, demographic, and behavioral data to deliver personalized tasks and dynamic feedback
Requires nurse-facilitated PBL discussions and trained staff with consistency assessments
constraints: Implementation requires considerable organizational and facilitation capacity and may be constrained by disparities in educational resources and learner preparedness
target_learners: female breast cancer patients in hospital care
examples: The trial delivered 24 sessions over 3 months (two per week, 45 min each) with monthly PBL group discussions facilitated by trained nursing staff.

As the authors report, "four major themes and eighteen sub-themes emerged from the data analysis namely: challenges related to nurse educators, challenges related to nursing students, challenges related to institutions or universities, and challenges related to PBL strategy". The PBL-strategy theme splits in Table 2 into case-related and assessment-related subthemes.

citation: Griffin A. (2025). The pivot to online teaching: an opportunity to create effective problem‐based learning environments for dietetic education. J Hum Nutr Diet. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.13378
title: Problem-based learning: four defining characteristics and an eight-step collaborative process
description: The article characterises PBL as grounded in experiential, collaborative, contextual and constructivist theories of learning, developed at McMaster University in the 1960s to promote student-centred, multidisciplinary education and lifelong learning. Most researchers agree all varieties share "the following four basic characteristics: (1) a focus on complex, real‐world problems that have no one 'correct' solution, (2) students work in groups, (3) students gain new information through self‐directed learning, and (4) educators act as facilitators". The article also enumerates an eight-step PBL process, from addressing realistic problems through applying prior knowledge, identifying learning gaps, discussing information sources, applying knowledge, and evaluating the learning experience.
requirements: Problems should be open-ended, complex and authentic, and contextualised for future or real workplaces
Educators act as facilitators who scaffold learning rather than provide the material needed to resolve the problem
constraints: The article cautions that PBL cannot be 'sprung' onto dietetic students who are practised in didactic styles of teaching and learning
examples: The article distinguishes PBL from case-based learning and discovery learning, citing Maudsley

title: Match PBL assessment to engagement in the process, self-directed learning, group participation, critical thinking and professional approach, aligned with module learning outcomes
description: The article argues that because traditional measures of academic achievement do not capture important differences in a student's ability to retrieve and apply acquired knowledge to real-life situations, "formative and summative assessments of PBL tutorials should be cognisant of the levels of engagement in the process, self‐directed learning, group participation, critical thinking and professional approach and align coherently with module learning outcomes including content knowledge". Assessment of PBL tutorials commonly focuses on how students go through the process and acquire self-study and thinking skills, and one important principle is matching the assessment method to the learning mode, developmental level, subject matter and programme outcomes.
requirements: Assessment must align coherently with module learning outcomes including content knowledge
constraints: The article presents this as an argument from the cited assessment literature, not as a tested result
examples: In the case study, both module leads marked the assignments and agreed grades, with reports structured as a technical report (engineers) and a reflection (dietitians)

article_title: Design and evaluation of a problem-based learning VR module for apparel fit correction training.
citation: Galada, Aditi and Baytar, Fatma. (2025). Design and evaluation of a problem-based learning VR module for apparel fit correction training. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0311587
title: PBL-VR desktop training module for apparel fit correction
description: A desktop VR training module built in Unity using garment simulations exported from Clo3D, teaching apparel fit correction through five iterative problem-solving tasks on a sleeveless top, slacks, a full-sleeve t-shirt, a sleeveless dress, and a skirt. For each fit issue users see "a brief explanation of the garment fit issue that needs to be rectified" and choose among "three potential pattern modification options one of which would correct the fit issue," with immediate audio-visual feedback explaining why a pattern change corrected the fit. It was designed following Experiential Learning Theory, Constructivist Learning Theory, and PBL theory, and was refined via a five-person expert pilot panel.
requirements: Learners need an introductory understanding of interpreting folds and draglines, so the module begins with an explanation of how draglines and folds originate and a short video on recognizing fit issues, plus a tutorial task on navigation

Authors state it can supplement but not replace physical garment fitting practice
target_learners: Novice apparel design students and college students without prerequisite patternmaking knowledge
target_learning_goals: Understanding of body-to-pattern relationships for varied body shapes
examples: A five-person fit expert panel piloted the modules and prompted changes such as adding a navigation tutorial, changing fabric colors so draglines and folds were visible, and eliminating excess at the pant front rise

title: Combined PBL-CBL teaching grounded in constructivist, cooperative learning, and situated cognition theories
description: The article presents the theoretical basis of combined PBL-CBL teaching as three theories: constructivist learning theory, under which "learning is a process of active knowledge construction by learners, rather than passive acceptance"; cooperative learning theory, emphasizing cooperation and mutual assistance among learners; and situated cognition theory, holding that knowledge is constructed and applied in specific contexts. The combined method is said to align with all three by having students actively explore real problems, discuss in groups, and analyze real cases in clinical contexts.
requirements: Instructors with sufficient expertise and teaching skills to guide discussions and analyses
constraints: Demands considerable student time and energy for self-directed study and collaborative discussions, challenging for students with weaker academic foundation or limited self-discipline

citation: Brown Jeffrey B. BS, Varadhan Ajay K. BS, Albers Jacob R. BA MS, Kudrimoti Shreyas BA, Cervantes Estelle MD, Sgobba Phillip MD MBS, Yenser Dawn M. C-TAGME, Kane Bryan G. MD. (2024). title: Three-digit codebook framework for qualitatively measuring the patient-care impact of resident EBM activity
description: The article provides "a framework for qualitative measurement of EBM research and application skills among learners." Each log's free-text answer to "Based on your research, would you have done anything differently?" was assigned a three-digit code: digit 1 whether research affected the current patient's care, digit 2 whether it would change future care, and digit 3 whether the change was in concordance with the researched evidence. constraints: Inter-rater reliability was not formally measured, and the authors note the qualitative methodology "introduced the possibility for interpretation bias in our results."

examples: Coders met to code the first 200 logs together to create a consensus for grading and met throughout the project to review logs with unclear coding.

title: PBL-based introductory graduate course in critical thinking and experimental design using COVID-19 problems
description: A first-semester course for matriculating biomedical doctoral students, delivered in small groups of four or five with mixed expertise, each guided by a faculty facilitator across 13 formal sessions. Consistent with the PBL tenet that "student learning is self-directed", students researched literature before sessions, a student leader managed discussion, and facilitators helped identify learning issues. Problem materials with student question guides and facilitator guides prepared for each session
constraints: Development of de novo COVID-19-based problems required extensive research under shifting scientific knowledge
Larger programs require more facilitators; facilitator training is a significant time commitment

description: The course organizes each problem into a repeating block: a background session, a hypothesis-development session where students "began to design experiments to test the hypothesis", and a final session fleshing out design details. Because students had "three opportunities to discuss hypothesis development, experimental design and analysis during sessions with their facilitators", the structure deliberately spaces practice of the target skills across problems. target_learning_goals: data interpretation and statistical analysis planning

constraints: Traditional PBL implementations face limits in securing space and time, which e-PBL addresses

citation: Chung Eva Yin-han. (2019). Facilitating learning of community-based rehabilitation through problem-based learning in higher education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1868-4
title: A six-step PBL framework with three learning phases for teaching CBR
description: The article's framework, built from a thematic synthesis of 14 articles on PBL, organises PBL as six steps: knowing the problem scenario, identifying facts, identifying knowledge gaps, developing resources, gaining insights into applying knowledge, and reflecting on knowledge gain. A tutor guides students through three major phases of learning: problem analysis, self-directed learning, and reporting. Knowledge acquisition comprises a discursive, theoretical, conceptual level and an active, practical, experiential level, and the framework "emphasize on learning" rather than problem solving alone, in contrast to the Maastricht seven-step model.
requirements: A tutor to guide students through the problem analysis, self-directed learning, and reporting phases, with consultation arrangements available
constraints: The framework was developed from a synthesis of PBL literature from 2008 to 2017 and tested only in CBR-related higher education courses

examples: The framework was derived from CINALHL and MEDLINE searches (2008-2017), of which 14 of 118 extracted articles were used for thematic analysis

title: A group work-based PBL protocol with checkpoints, e-portfolios, and a final debate across a 13-week semester
description: The protocol is a group work-based, learner-centred, problem-oriented teaching design implemented over a single 13-week semester. Course content is divided into modules presented as checkpoints; students form groups of six, analyse assigned real-world problem scenarios, generate hypotheses, pursue self-directed study, and present at each checkpoint, with all work recorded in e-portfolios. The final presentation is followed by an open forum or debate to consolidate learning. Assessment is holistic and performance-based, using e-portfolio rubrics covering content relevance, knowledge integration, and clarity and accuracy of concepts and theories.

constraints: Practical skills developed in PBL cannot be sufficiently assessed through traditional paper-based examination, per the article

description: The article recommends that PBL counter the first critique of isolation by making context-specific skills more prominent, since "Only within a specific context do certain skills, and their use, attain relevance." article_title: Problem solving skills versus knowledge acquisition: the historical dispute that split problem-based learning into two camps.
citation: Servant-Miklos, V. F. C. (2018). Problem solving skills versus knowledge acquisition: the historical dispute that split problem-based learning into two camps. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(3), 619–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-018-9835-0
title: Two models of problem-based learning: the Knowledge Acquisition model and the Problem-Solving Skills model
description: The article organizes the history of PBL around two divergent models issuing from the 1969 McMaster programme. Type 1 curricula ask students to generate a "mental model" of phenomena underlying a problem (the Knowledge Acquisition model), while Type 2 curricula have students "play doctor", focusing on "problem-solving and clinical reasoning skills" (the Problem-Solving Skills model). The paper shows this split originated in the divergent cognitive psychologies of Barrows and Schmidt. It is used as the organizing framework for the whole historical analysis.

constraints: The taxonomy is drawn from Schmidt et al. (2009) as reported by this historical paper, and concerns medical-school PBL curricula
