target_learning_goals: acquisition and understanding of biomedical knowledge
examples: The paper distinguishes the majority Problem-Solving Skills curricula from a substantial minority of Knowledge Acquisition curricula among over 500 medical schools using some form of PBL

title: Problem-based learning as student-centered pedagogy with small groups, non-directive tutors and authentic tasks
description: The article defines PBL as "a student-centered pedagogy in which participants are allocated in groups of up to 8 persons under non-directive tutors and given tasks or challenges that reflect situations relevant to the working environments they will experience". In this way learners are empowered to integrate theory and practice and apply knowledge and skills to develop viable solutions. It contrasts with lecture-based learning, which focuses on factual knowledge and memorization with little chance for application.

Tasks or challenges reflecting relevant working situations

article_title: PBL 2.0: enhancing problem-based learning through increased student participation.
citation: Wiznia Daniel, Korom Robert, Marzuk Peter, Safdieh Joseph, Grafstein Bernice. (2012). PBL 2.0: enhancing problem-based learning through increased student participation. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.3402/meo.v17i0.17375
title: PBL 2.0: a revised problem-based learning format with reduced objectives, pair/trio-led discussions, and no lectures
description: PBL 2.0 is a revised PBL format implemented in the 11-week Brain and Mind course at Weill Cornell, meeting "for 90 min two times per week" in 10 groups of 10 second-year students with faculty facilitators. Learning objectives were "reduced through deletion and consolidation (from 10 to between 4 and 6)"; pairs/trios led interactive discussions using talking points posed to the group, with lectures, PowerPoint, and extensive handouts prohibited, and computers banned on the first day to preserve problem-solving. Facilitators corrected errors and managed time without dominating sessions, and grading emphasized contributions to discussion.
requirements: Faculty and student orientations on the new format and amended evaluation expectations
Facilitators instructed to evaluate students on contributions to group problem solving and discussion stimulation rather than stock lectures
The same amount of classroom time as the prior format
constraints: Twenty percent of respondents reported no adherence at all to the model
Some long-serving faculty facilitators had difficulty transitioning to the new model
Evaluated in a single second-year medical neuroscience course without randomization
target_learning_goals: acquisition and discussion of biomedical learning objectives
interactive group learning of neuroscience, neuroanatomy, pharmacology, clinical neurology, and psychiatry topics
examples: In the Brain and Mind course, one student served as reader and another as scribe organizing details on the whiteboard; on day two, pairs/trios formulated 4 or 5 key talking points posed verbally or via whiteboards.

title: PBL 2.0 design pattern: prepare-all-objectives plus pair/trio-led interactive discussion
description: A reusable lesson-level design in which every student prepares all of a case's learning objectives while a small pair/trio leads an interactive discussion of one objective each. The authors state "we encourage students to prepare all learning objectives so students can contribute meaningfully to discussions," and that "PBL thrives when students solve problems in an interactive environment." Reducing objectives to 4–6 makes universal preparation realistic, and prohibiting lectures shifts presenters from delivering information to posing discussion points.
requirements: Learning objectives reduced and consolidated to a number pairs/trios and the whole group can realistically prepare
Explicit orientation of faculty and students to the new expectations
Assessment incentives aligned with discussion contribution rather than presentation quality
constraints: Involves more work outside of the classroom for students
Requires facilitators to refrain from lecturing and to note students who fail to prepare
target_learners: small-group learners in medical or higher education
target_learning_goals: preparation across all of a case's learning objectives
examples: In Brain and Mind, objectives were cut from 10 to between 4 and 6, and each pair/trio formulated 4 or 5 key talking points posed to the group without PowerPoint or handouts.

title: Increased participation as the key mechanism of effective problem-based learning
description: The authors' explanatory account of why PBL works and why it had gone stale: "the key ingredient is increased participation," with engagement in dynamic, interactive problem solving while working through a case. In the pre-intervention format students over-prepared their own individual presentations and 'tuned out' during peers' presentations; PBL 2.0 restores interaction by requiring universal preparation of all objectives, so students must bolster their fund of knowledge before day-two discussions. The authors frame this as a return to the team-oriented problem-solving origins of PBL.
requirements: All students must be prepared to discuss the learning objectives for the case for interaction to occur
constraints: The authors present this as their interpretation of one course's experience, not a tested mechanism; objective learning assessment was not conducted
target_learning_goals: comprehension and retention of case-related concepts
examples: The authors state PBL had become ritualized, with students delivering overly detailed presentations and lacking the knowledge to discuss peers' presentations.

BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-53
title: Four-day small-group problem-based learning workshop for practicing general practitioners
description: A CME intervention in which an expert PBL tutor led physicians through clinical case studies covering nine priority health programs, running 4 days at 8 hours per day. The article describes PBL as "an action-reflection-action process in which GPs identify problems from 'clinical cases'" followed by information search and hypothesis formulation. Each session used Schmidt's seven steps split into a discussion meeting, individual study time, and a concluding meeting, with case materials distributed 8 days in advance.
requirements: An educational professional with PBL expertise as tutor, a program expert as chair, clinical case studies designed from real and simulated patients, and access to a library with electronic resources for individual study
constraints: The study used small groups of 9 physicians, and the authors note restrictions on sample size are common in such studies
target_learning_goals: improved clinical competence across cognitive, habitual behavioral and affective dimensions in nine priority health programs
examples: Sessions lasted approximately 3.5 hours per health program: 1.5 hours for the discussion meeting completing the first 5 of Schmidt's steps, 1 hour of individual study (step 6), and 1 hour for the concluding meeting (step 7)
